I am 51 years old and have farmed these 5 mu in Quzhou for 30 years. My household is just me and my wife, and we both pick up off-farm work when we can, so I have to be careful with labor. I have a well, which means I can pump water when the crops need it, but I do not waste electricity on unnecessary irrigation.

My cropping system is cotton, but with only two of us to do the work, I keep cotton to 1 mu. It is labor-intensive — planting with plastic film, spraying, and especially picking all take hands. I will rotary till that plot and sow my kangchongmian (Bt cotton) around early April. I will put down 80 jin of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer as basal dressing. Cotton does not need much water, so I will irrigate only once during the season, but I will watch the weather. Even with Bt cotton, aphids and mites come, so I will spray insecticide about nine times and herbicide once — roughly ten applications in total. I also apply growth regulators to keep the plants from getting too tall. I expect about 550 jin of seed cotton per mu, which gives me steady cash.

On the other 4 mu, I have winter wheat already in the ground from last autumn. I sowed improved variety seeds at 30 jin per mu after rotary tilling. Now, at the start of the growing season, I will topdress with urea when the wheat greens up. The wheat gets three irrigations — winter water, jointing stage, and grain filling — all from the well. I spray once for insects and once for weeds. I expect about 1100 jin per mu at harvest in early June. I keep most of it for our own flour.

Immediately after the wheat comes off, I plant summer maize on the same 4 mu. I use Weike 118 hybrid seed. I do not till — I plant directly into the stubble to save time and labor before the summer rains arrive. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing. I irrigate three times if the weather is dry, and I spray three times for insects plus once for weeds. I expect about 1250 jin per mu by September. This rotation has never failed me.

I stick to this plan because it balances cash and grain with the labor I have. Cotton pays well but takes time; wheat and maize feed us and bring in extra income without needing me in the field every single day.
